_comment: Key lessons. Pass 23 replaced the Pass 6 set of 10 with this set of 15, implementing LESSON_AUDIT.md §6 — the Pass 22 convergence audit that scored every prior lesson against the three lessons-learned references now committed in docs/references/. Each lesson points at real assets already on the map so it can be demonstrated rather than just asserted; clicking one frames those assets in the 3D view. `doctrine_ref` names the section of docs/doctrine.md the framing comes from and `source_tag` uses that file's sourcing key, both unchanged from Pass 6. `corpus_support` (new, Pass 23) is the separate, stricter question the audit asked: how many of the three independent lessons-learned references actually carry this finding — CONVERGENT-3 means all three reached it independently, SINGLE-SOURCE means one did, UNSUPPORTED means the claim rests entirely on sources outside that corpus and the lesson says so in its own text. `contested`/`caution` (new, Pass 23) mark findings the corpus itself warns against over-reading. NOTHING RENDERS corpus_support, contested or caution yet — they are carried in data so the distinction isn't silently lost, and UI treatment is future work (docs/BACKLOG.md). Every lesson's `connection_types` was verified against the edges that actually exist between that lesson's own assets; see PASS23_HANDOFF.md for the reconciliation table.

lessons.title: Drones are the connective tissue, not a category
lessons.summary: One cheap airframe type now does reconnaissance, strike, deep strike, resupply and air defence — it is the layer every other category runs through.
lessons.detail: This is the finding all three reference documents lead with, reached independently from three different source bases. The Russian-side reference puts it plainly: every source in its corpus 'treats UAV presence as the dominant fact of the battlefield rather than one input among many,' and one platform type now crosses five traditional domain lines — reconnaissance, precision strike, electronic warfare, logistics, information operations, even air-to-air intercept. The Western-side reference reaches the same place from NATO's institutional literature: multi-domain integration is 'not a future-force aspiration in the current literature but a description of how both sides are already fighting.' The Ukrainian-side reference supplies the structural proof: Ukraine stood up the Unmanned Systems Forces as an independent branch in February 2024 and an Unmanned Air Defence Forces element inside the Air Force — a state reorganising its order of battle around the drone layer. The uncomfortable corollary, which this tool should own rather than hide: the Russian reference states that 'any platform or curriculum still treating drones as a subtopic under ISR or fires is organized around a battlefield that no longer exists' — and this map's own category filter does exactly that, filing drones as uav-reconnaissance and uav-strike alongside artillery and armour as peers. Read the categories on this map as a legacy convenience, not as how the fighting is organised. The five assets here are deliberately one side's drone layer plus the gun built to fight it: an Orlan-10 finding, a Lancet striking, a Shahed reaching the deep rear, an Omich-2 carrying supplies forward, and a Gepard trying to deny all of it.
lessons.doctrine_ref: §5 FPV tactical pattern taxonomy / §6 Force structure pattern
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-3 — independently supported in all three lessons-learned references. The Ukrainian document names its own convergence with the Western one explicitly.

lessons.title: Detectability, not distance, decides survivability
lessons.summary: This map is a distance ruler. The strongest finding in the reference corpus is that distance is no longer what keeps you alive.
lessons.detail: The Western-side reference states it as its own through-line: 'detectability, not distance, is now the primary determinant of survivability' for command and control nodes. The mechanism is specific — Ukrainian doctrine prioritises basements and underground positions because they mask electromagnetic emissions as well as providing overhead protection, treats visible administrative buildings as pre-plotted targets to be actively avoided, and understands that a high-power transmission draws fire within roughly fifteen minutes. Deception is doctrine, not improvisation: decoy antennas, simulated vehicle parks and staged signs of habitation exist to make the enemy spend precision munitions on empty ground. The Ukrainian-side reference arrives at the same conclusion down a completely different source line, and says so itself — its command-post finding is 'the same conclusion the Western-side document reaches from the CALL/TDF manual, independently arrived at from a different Ukrainian source line.' Its mechanism is architectural: split commander, operator and administrator functions across separate workstations feeding a shared field server rather than concentrating everything on one operator, and rank comms by reliability under contact rather than bandwidth — tactical radio, then relay, then directional satellite, with the highest-bandwidth option ranked last on purpose. The slower detection pattern this lesson replaced is real and still worth knowing: both sides map a battalion sector's drone positions over two to seven days by following returning drones home rather than shooting them down. But that is the patient end of the same problem. The fast end is fifteen minutes from pressing transmit. Read every distance on this map as a starting condition, not as protection.
lessons.doctrine_ref: §3 Detection as pattern-of-life / §2 Distance / echelon structure
lessons.source_tag: [Western §3.2; Ukrainian §3.2; Russian §3.2, §4; Combat Exp. RU, Appendix 9]
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-3 — the Ukrainian reference explicitly names its own independent convergence with the Western reference's §3.2 on this exact finding.

lessons.title: Control of the lower sky sets how close you can stand
lessons.summary: Disposition depth is decided by local drone superiority, not by doctrine or preference.
lessons.detail: The side holding control of the lower sky can deploy 1–1.5 km from the line and use direct-fire tank positions; the side without it is pushed back to roughly 7 km and restricted to indirect fire. Sourcing note, because it matters more than the figures do: that pair of numbers comes from Markin's Russian-side combat-experience notebook via docs/doctrine.md §2, and it appears in none of the three lessons-learned references. The Russian-side reference's own reading note says to treat that source's specific numbers as 'illustrative, not statistical.' So read 1–1.5 km versus 7 km as one practitioner's account of one sector, not as a measured constant — and note that the assets below sit at their own sourced distances (Leopard 2 at 2.6 km, T-72 at 4.4 km), which do not reproduce that spread and are not intended to. What the corpus does support, strongly, is the principle underneath: classical distance-based safety has stopped governing disposition. The Western reference's 'detectability, not distance' finding and Zaluzhnyi's naming of air and EW capacity among the levers for breaking positional deadlock both point the same way. Worth holding alongside lesson 2, which points somewhere subtly different about what to do: the Western corpus says survivability is bought with emissions discipline, camouflage and deception; this lesson says depth is set by who owns the air above it. Both are true and they are not the same instruction. Shown here: the reconnaissance drones that are the actual object of the contest, and the counter-UAS systems each side uses to deny the other the lower sky.
lessons.corpus_support: Principle: CONVERGENT-2 (Western §3.2, Ukrainian §2). The specific 1–1.5 km vs. 7 km figures: SINGLE-SOURCE, from docs/doctrine.md's Markin notebook, carried in no reference document.
lessons.caution: The 1–1.5 km / 7 km pair is practitioner testimony from one notebook covering one sector, not a measured or replicated figure. The Russian-side reference explicitly says to treat that source's numbers as illustrative rather than statistical. The principle is well supported; the numbers are one account.

lessons.title: Reconnaissance and fires fused into one function
lessons.summary: Finding and shooting stopped being two jobs handed between two staffs. The doctrinal boundary between them no longer describes how either side fights.
lessons.detail: The supported finding is structural rather than temporal: reconnaissance and fires have fused. The Russian-side reference records the U.S. Army's own read that Russian 'Fires' and 'Intelligence' functions 'have become inseparable from UAV reconnaissance-strike integration, to the point that the traditional warfighting-function boundaries in U.S. doctrine don't map cleanly onto how Russian units now operate.' The Western reference treats precision fires, reduced force mass and robotic systems as 'a single interconnected shift rather than separate domain stories.' That fusion — one loop rather than two functions with a handoff between them — is what the connected chain below shows: a Leleka-100 cueing both a gun line and a man-portable loitering munition, with the firing position itself in the picture rather than implied. On timing, be careful. The familiar framing — call-for-fire took hours, now it takes single-digit minutes — comes from docs/doctrine.md §1 and appears in none of the three reference documents. It is plausible and widely reported, but it is not corpus-supported, and docs/doctrine.md's own caveat cuts against the heroic version: a former Ukrainian FPV operator describes strikes still taking 30+ minutes, with the time lost to deconfliction overhead rather than jamming. Treat 'minutes' as the achievable case on a good day in a good sector, not as the standing state. The guns here are deliberately the responsive ones — M777, Bohdana, Caesar — rather than HIMARS, which is a deep-strike interdiction system running its own separate targeting chain against pre-planned high-value targets and does not illustrate a squad-range sensor-to-shooter loop.
lessons.source_tag: [Russian §3.1; Western §3.7; web: Dignitas, Modern Diplomacy, MWI]
lessons.corpus_support: Mechanism (recon/fires fusion): CONVERGENT-2 (Russian §3.1, Western §3.7). Headline timing figure ('hours to minutes'): UNSUPPORTED — stated in no reference document; rests on docs/doctrine.md §1 alone.

lessons.title: Kill chains pushed to squad level — and command culture hasn't followed
lessons.summary: A squad with its own drones is a complete sensor-to-shooter loop. The command structures above it were not designed to let go.
lessons.detail: Half of this lesson is the part everyone repeats: authority to complete a kill chain has moved down rather than concentrating at higher HQ. The Russian-side reference records units 'forced into smaller teams, faster low-level decision-making, and more flexible logistics because massed formations are now visible and targetable almost immediately' — assault groups down to 3–5 personnel, strongpoints becoming dispersed two-man positions. The Western reference notes most 2023 counteroffensive fighting happened at brigade, battalion and even company level rather than the division/corps level earlier doctrine assumed. The other half is the part that usually gets dropped, and the references insist on it. The Russian document flags that Russian command culture remains 'highly centralized and rigid' by design — a matter of doctrine, not adaptation failure — 'creating friction with the small-unit independence that survival now requires.' Its practitioner sources complain about the same tension from inside: bypassed chains of command, units hoarding drones instead of pooling reconnaissance, and incentive structures that reward video-friendly kills over units actually holding ground. That last one is the counter-intuitive failure mode worth carrying: the technology rewards decentralisation and the accounting system rewards spectacle, and they are not the same thing. The reference's own verdict on teaching this lesson without its second half is blunt — 'training that teaches drone tactics without addressing delegation of authority to the team level is solving half the problem.' The assets are deliberately one side's loop rather than a mix of both: a Russian squad, its reconnaissance and strike drones, its squad-level terminal, and the tactical command post the authority is supposed to be devolving away from.
lessons.source_tag: [Russian §3.2; Western §4; Ukrainian §3.7; web: Small Wars Journal — Distributed Combat Power]
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-2 — Russian §3.2 and Western §4 both carry it, including the command-culture friction. Ukrainian §3.7's new-branch rationale is adjacent structural evidence rather than a direct match.

lessons.title: Logistics risk became a subset of counter-drone risk
lessons.summary: Resupply and casualty evacuation stopped being logistics problems with a threat overlay. They are counter-drone problems now.
lessons.detail: All three references reach this independently. The Russian-side reference is the most explicit: robotic ground platforms and heavy drones are increasingly used for resupply and casualty evacuation 'specifically because manned logistics runs are now one of the highest-casualty activities on the battlefield,' and it names the coupling directly — 'logistics risk is now largely a subset of counter-UAV risk, not a separate problem.' The Western reference describes the doctrinal response from the other side of the line: smaller, dispersed logistics task forces trading efficiency for survivability against UAS, long-range fires and EW. The Ukrainian reference reaches the same structural pressure and names its own parallel to the Russian finding, but records a different first-line fix — units systematically underestimate reset time between missions, and the documented answer is pre-staging fuel, ammunition and comms at the home base rather than robotic substitution. Two responses to one problem, which is what makes the underlying coupling convincing rather than fashionable. The setting matters too: persistent drone coverage dominates a band roughly 30 km either side of the line, and while that specific figure comes from docs/doctrine.md rather than any reference document, the consequence is the thing this lesson is about. The two forward casualty collection points show the cost — their own sourced copy describes drone coverage erasing the assumption of a safe evacuation route for the first 10–15 km, which is why they are built small and hidden rather than large and well-equipped. The five unmanned ground vehicles show the response: the run that used to take a truck and a crew now takes a machine, on both sides.
lessons.doctrine_ref: §2 Distance / echelon structure / §6 Force structure pattern
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-3 — Russian §3.3 states the coupling outright, Western §3.3 documents the dispersal response independently, and Ukrainian §3.3 names its own parallel to the Russian finding while recording a different first-line fix.

lessons.title: Counter-drone is an integration problem, not a hardware problem
lessons.summary: Every source in the corpus names counter-drone as the clearest capability gap. None of them describes it as a shortage of equipment.
lessons.detail: The Western-side reference names the shortfalls specifically: limited interoperability between allied counter-UAS systems, incomplete capability coverage across the threat spectrum, weak platform survivability, and gaps in personnel training and intelligence-processing capacity. Its verdict for training commands is unusually direct — the integration gap, 'not a hardware gap, is the most actionable, multiply-corroborated curriculum fix identified across sources,' because 'training that assumes systems will be fielded individually rather than as a networked detect-track-defeat chain is solving the wrong problem.' The Russian-side reference reports the same gap from inside its own corpus: counter-UAV 'remains fragmented and under-resourced at the unit level relative to the offensive drone ecosystem across every source — the clearest capability gap, and the one most consistently self-reported by the practitioner sources.' The Ukrainian-side reference closes the loop and flags the convergence itself as the signal: its own peer-reviewed military-technical journals still treat coordinated counter-drone response as an open research question, which matches a Western institutional finding that Ukraine's counter-drone effort 'lacks a single point of mission accountability and is fragmented across services' — 'one of the stronger three-document convergences in the whole corpus, because none of the three sources involved were checking the others' work.' Two things follow for this map. First, the assets below are not a solution; they are a set of individually capable systems whose value depends entirely on the chain they are or are not part of — which is why the three side_a systems all connect to a single fusion node and that node is the actual subject of the lesson. Second, note what is missing: side_b has no battle-management node on this map at all. That asymmetry is a roster gap, not a claim about Russian capability, and it is logged as such.
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-3 — and the Ukrainian reference itself calls this one of the strongest three-document convergences in the corpus.
lessons.caution: Do not read Ukraine's counter-drone effort as a solved model to copy. The Western reference is explicit that this gap 'is not fully closed even on the Ukrainian side' and is 'a genuinely new organizational problem rather than a solved one being exported wholesale.'

lessons.title: EW is the invisible battlefield everything else depends on
lessons.summary: Sensors, drones and comms only work if the electromagnetic fight is being won — and doctrine on both sides now assumes it is being lost.
lessons.detail: All three references carry this. The Western-side document supplies the sharpest single consequence: Excalibur 155mm GPS-guided rounds 'have suffered accuracy degradation from Russian EW jamming, forcing reliance on non-GPS-guided fires or renewed emphasis on jam-resistant guidance in follow-on procurement' — a precision munition degraded into an ordinary one by an effect nobody can see, which is why an M777 sits in this lesson alongside the jammers. The Ukrainian-side reference shows how far this has travelled into design: the AFU's own unmanned-crew manual treats analogue and mechanical fallback — dual GPS/GLONASS cross-checking, mandatory compass, sun and star navigation skill, a scripted lost-signal algorithm — as 'the default design baseline, not a contingency: Ukrainian doctrine assumes the primary electromagnetic system will be denied.' Its comms doctrine says the same thing about bandwidth: PACE planning ranks tactical radio first and omnidirectional satellite last, deliberately, on reliability under contact rather than throughput — which is worth reading against the Starlink terminal shown here, the highest-bandwidth and lowest-ranked option in that scheme. The Russian-side reference adds the organisational failure mode both sides share: units often hold electronic countermeasure equipment without the trained personnel to maintain or employ it correctly. Two further details from docs/doctrine.md are worth keeping with their sourcing attached rather than dropping: passive RF triangulation at 5–20 m accuracy [DW], and the finding that decentralised jammer procurement creates uncoordinated 'unofficial EW fields' that degrade friendly drone performance as much as enemy drones [Combat Exp. RU]. Neither figure is carried in any reference document.
lessons.source_tag: [Russian §3.4, §3.5; Western §3.4; Ukrainian §3.2, §3.4; DW; Combat Exp. RU]
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-3 — Russian §3.4/§3.5, Western §3.4 and Ukrainian §3.2/§3.4 all carry it independently. The 5–20 m triangulation accuracy figure and the 'unofficial EW fields' finding are SINGLE-SOURCE from docs/doctrine.md and are attributed inline.

lessons.title: Fibre-optic links: when both sides reach the same fix, the adaptation is structural
lessons.summary: A spool of glass defeats the entire soft-kill EW layer. The transferable lesson is not the spool — it is that independent convergence is how you tell a real adaptation from a fashionable one.
lessons.detail: This is the best-evidenced lesson on this map, and the reason is worth more than the technology. A fibre-optic control link is immune to RF jamming: the dominant countermeasure simply stops applying, at some cost to manoeuvrability and a finite spool. But both finished references flag the convergence itself as the finding rather than the capability. The Russian-side reference calls it 'a case where a single technical fix has forced a doctrinal response across multiple institutions simultaneously — a useful marker of which adaptations are structural versus which are still improvised.' The Western-side reference says the same thing about method: fibre-optic FPVs appear 'independently as an adaptation across Western, Ukrainian, and Russian sources, which is a strong signal that this is a structural response to the EW environment rather than a one-sided innovation.' The Ukrainian-side reference supplies the timeline the other two could only gesture at: Russia fielded fibre-optic FPVs first, in the Kursk region from around August 2024, specifically to defeat Ukrainian jamming; Ukraine's Ministry of Defence began certifying domestic fibre-optic models within months, with first Brave1 test flights in late March 2025 and roughly 40 certified models by that April. Its own conclusion is the portable one: 'a single technical fix, adopted by one side under pressure, was replicated by the other side inside about six months, which is a useful marker for how fast a genuinely effective adaptation propagates across a contested front, regardless of who invents it.' Six months is the number to remember — it is the shelf life of a capability advantage. Ukraine is also pursuing a second, distinct route to the same jamming immunity: FPVs guided by onboard machine vision rather than a physical tether, described in the record as immature but active, alongside fibre optic rather than replacing it. Two honest notes. No aircraft-type FPV strike drone with a documented fibre-optic option exists on this map yet — a known content gap — so the mechanism is shown through the two ground robots that do document a real fibre option on either side, alongside the jammers a fibre link routes around. And on range, this map disagrees with one of its own sources: the Western reference calls fibre-optic FPVs 'short-ranged,' while the distance ruler's separately-sourced 2025–2026 marker puts the practical working envelope at ~20 km against radio FPV's ~10 km, with extended coils reported far beyond. The marker is the later claim and the map follows it, but the disagreement is real and named rather than smoothed over.
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-3 — the strongest-evidenced lesson in this set. Russian §3.4 and Western §3.4 both flag the independent convergence as the signal; Ukrainian §3.4 supplies the ~6-month replication timeline that makes the convergence concrete rather than asserted.

lessons.title: Consumption rates, not inventories, decide sustainment
lessons.summary: A single FPV company can burn through ~7,200 munitions a month. Heavy multirotors survive 5–10 missions.
lessons.detail: Illustrative unit economics (a Lithuanian projection grounded in Ukrainian usage rates, not Ukrainian actuals): one FPV company at intensive tempo consumes roughly 7,200 kamikaze drones per month, and a heavy 'Baba Yaga'-type multirotor typically survives only 5–10 missions before loss. Planning against an inventory number rather than a monthly burn rate is how a drone programme runs dry in its second month. The corpus supports the framing even where it does not carry these particular figures: the Russian-side reference concludes that procurement and industrial-base questions 'are now inseparable from tactical questions — a battlefield technology with a consumer-electronics supply chain changes acquisition timelines in ways traditional defense procurement cycles aren't built for.' The Ukrainian-side reference describes the institutional answer, where battlefield performance converts directly into equipment allocation within weeks rather than through a written report. The connected pair shown here — Russia's Lancet drawing airframes and batteries from its own near-rear logistics point — is the one complete, data-backed resupply chain on the map for this; Ukraine's own forward distribution hub is included alongside it as the equivalent chokepoint on the other side, since the burn-rate figure itself is sourced to Ukrainian usage even though no individual Ukrainian strike-drone-to-hub connection is modelled yet.
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-2 — Russian §4 and Ukrainian §3.6 both treat consumption and procurement as tactical variables. The specific 7,200/month and 5–10 mission figures are SINGLE-SOURCE (a Lithuanian projection), and the lesson says so in its own first sentence.

lessons.title: The cheapest system destroys the most expensive
lessons.summary: A drone costing tens of thousands routinely kills a vehicle costing millions — in both directions, on both sides.
lessons.detail: This is the procurement argument in one line, and the map shows it as two mirrored pairs rather than one: Russia's Lancet (~$35K) against Ukraine's Leopard 2 (~$9–10M), and Ukraine's Switchblade 300 (~$38K) against Russia's T-72 (~$2.0–2.5M). Neither pairing claims a specific engagement happened — it is a cost-tile comparison, not a battle report — but both directions of the asymmetry are on the map, not just the one that suits a particular audience. Two orders of magnitude between the thing spent and the thing destroyed is what makes mass-produced expendables a strategic argument rather than a tactical convenience, and it is why lesson 10's burn-rate framing matters more than any inventory figure. What this lesson deliberately no longer claims: the widely-quoted figure that 60–70% of equipment losses on both sides are now attributable to drones. That number is real reporting and probably directionally right, but the Pass 22 audit found the reference corpus actively warns against exactly this class of claim, so it now lives in the caution below and in lesson 15 rather than in a headline. The cost asymmetry is what these four assets can actually demonstrate; an attribution statistic across a 1,200 km front is not.
lessons.corpus_support: Cost asymmetry: CONVERGENT-2 — Russian §3.1 and Western §3.1 both treat cheap drones destroying expensive platforms as the dominant economic fact. The separate '60–70% of equipment losses' attribution statistic is CONTRADICTED by the corpus's own methodological caution and has been removed from the claim; see caution.
lessons.caution: The '60–70% of equipment losses caused by drones' figure was the headline of this lesson before Pass 23. It is stated in none of the three reference documents, and the Western reference's visibility-bias warning targets precisely this claim type: viral, well-filmed drone strikes 'generate outsized claims of systemic effectiveness relative to the much larger number of undocumented failures.' The denominator — all equipment losses, including undocumented ones — is the quantity that warning says is systematically under-observed. Treat the direction as sound and the precision as unknowable. See lesson 15.

lessons.title: The deep rear stopped being a sanctuary
lessons.summary: Cheap one-way systems reach targets thousands of kilometres behind the line.
lessons.detail: Depth used to buy safety: past a few hundred kilometres, an asset was effectively out of reach of anything but strategic systems. Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb reached airfields roughly 4,300 km from the front using smuggled short-range drones launched locally — the reach came from defeating border security rather than from any airframe's range. The consequence for this map is that the deepest band is no longer a rear area in the traditional sense: power generation, logistics hubs and airfields are all now inside somebody's reach. Sourcing note, stated plainly because this lesson is weaker than its neighbours on exactly this point: none of the three lessons-learned references mentions this operation, truck-smuggled launch, or strategic-depth strike by short-range systems at all. The claim rests entirely on docs/doctrine.md §2's bare [web] tag — the weakest citation in that file, with no named outlet, unlike the [web: Small Wars Journal] or [web: US Army TDF lessons] tags elsewhere in it. The operation is widely and credibly reported and this lesson is very probably true; it simply has not been through the same three-document convergence check the rest of this set has, and should not be read with the same confidence as lesson 9. The two strategic infrastructure targets at 220 km and 250 km carry the point; the 80 km forward distribution hub that used to sit here has been removed, because no strategic-rear-band (200+ km) logistics asset exists on this map yet and using the deepest available stand-in required more caveat than it was worth.
lessons.corpus_support: UNSUPPORTED — no meaningful support in any of the three lessons-learned references. Retained because the underlying reporting is credible and the map already models the capability, but flagged here so it is not read at the same confidence as the CONVERGENT-3 lessons.

lessons.title: Standardisation, not volume, is the coalition ammunition constraint
lessons.summary: Matching calibre does not guarantee usable ammunition across a coalition. Fuzes, propellant and shell bodies decide that.
lessons.detail: Scope note first, because it changes how this should be read: this is the one lesson in the set carried by a single reference document, and structurally so rather than by oversight — a single-nation producer has no coalition standardisation problem, so this finding could not be convergent by construction. The Western-side reference records that pre-war combined NATO 155mm production was roughly 300,000 rounds/year, and that by 2026 combined EU/UK/Ukrainian output is reported in the 1.2–3 million/year range depending on source and on how 'capacity' versus 'actual output' is counted, with a US Army Inspector General report noting the US portion fell short of its own targets. But the less-publicised finding is the more actionable one: even matched calibre production does not guarantee usable ammunition across a coalition, because 'fuze, propellant, and shell-body standards vary enough between NATO producers that STANAG-level standardization, not just factory throughput, is the binding constraint on ammunition interoperability in a multi-national force.' For policymakers the reference is explicit that the standardisation gap, not raw production volume, 'is the more actionable near-term acquisition lever.' The same document adds a related planning factor from the NATO curriculum guide: a unit fielding several NATO-standard and legacy Soviet-standard platforms cannot be treated as fungible with a unit fielding only one type. Ukraine's own defence-tech ecosystem is the instructive counter-case rather than a confirmation — a domestic production loop where the binding constraint is a different one entirely. Shown here: four 155mm systems from four different national production lines — American, German, French and Ukrainian — drawing from a single forward ammunition point. Same calibre, four sets of national standards behind it.
lessons.corpus_support: SINGLE-SOURCE (Western §3.5) — and structurally so, not by oversight: a single-nation producer has no coalition standardisation problem, so this finding cannot be convergent by construction. Read it as a Western-coalition-specific lesson, not a claim about how both sides fight.

lessons.title: The speed of the learning loop is itself the capability
lessons.summary: When a lesson reaches production in weeks instead of a doctrine revision cycle, the loop stops being administration and becomes a weapon.
lessons.detail: This is the finding the Ukrainian-side reference leads on, and the one place in the corpus where it is the primary rather than corroborating source. Its account of Brave1's e-Points marketplace describes a system that 'converts battlefield performance directly into equipment allocation within weeks: units earn points for verified kills and re-spend them on whichever certified system is currently working, and manufacturers see unit-level performance data directly' — which it characterises as 'functionally a lessons-learned process that skips the written report entirely and acts on the data.' The reference attaches its own caveat and it travels with the claim: the specific figures are self-reported by the ministries involved and not independently audited, so the mechanism is the well-supported part, not the numbers. Alongside it, Ukraine's formal lessons-learned doctrine standardised an after-action format that two independent unit-level sources were already using before the doctrine existed — 'itself a teaching point about how fast bottom-up practice can outpace top-down doctrine.' Zaluzhnyi's argument that doctrine needs continuous revision rather than periodic replacement describes the same pattern from the top. The Russian-side reference corroborates the pressure from its own direction: a battlefield technology with a consumer-electronics supply chain 'changes acquisition timelines in ways traditional defense procurement cycles aren't built for.' Read this against lesson 9's six-month replication window and the two become one argument — if a capability advantage lasts about half a year, then the rate at which an organisation learns is worth more than any particular thing it has learned. The four assets are Ukraine's own domestic deep-strike lineage, each successive design pushing range further: a volunteer project that reached serial production, a state aerospace manufacturer pivoting from airliners, the type that established the template, and the newest and longest-reaching. No asset on this map represents the institution behind that lineage — no drone school, acceleration cluster or training centre exists in the roster yet — which is a known gap, not an omission.
lessons.corpus_support: CONVERGENT-2, Ukrainian-primary — Ukrainian §3.6/§3.7/§4 carry it directly and Russian §4 corroborates the procurement-timeline pressure. The Ukrainian reference's own caveat about self-reported, unaudited figures is carried into the lesson text.

lessons.title: Some of what you have learned about this war is selection effect
lessons.summary: Well-filmed drone strikes travel. The failures don't. Curricula built from viral footage learn the exceptional case.
lessons.detail: This is a lesson about how to read the other fourteen, including where this platform has got it wrong. The Western-side reference carries an explicit methodological warning from the Australian Army Research Centre: 'viral, well-filmed drone strikes generate outsized claims of systemic effectiveness relative to the much larger number of undocumented failures' — and treats it as a training-design lesson in its own right, since 'curricula built primarily from social-media footage will be skewed toward exceptional cases.' The reference applies that caution to its own corpus, 'including this one.' The Russian-side reference reaches the same discipline from a different angle in its reliability notes: its practitioner sources are 'rich in detail but reflect individual experience and morale-building intent; treat specific numbers as illustrative, not statistical.' The worked example is this platform's own. Until Pass 23, lesson 11 on this map led with the claim that drones cause 60–70% of equipment losses, stated flatly, with no hedge — a hard percentage across a 1,200 km front, both sides, four years, whose denominator is precisely the quantity the AARC says goes systematically unobserved. It was the most quotable line in the lesson set and the least defensible. Three practical tests, transferable to anything else you read about this war. Ask what the denominator is and whether anyone could have counted it. Ask whether the claim's evidence base is the same thing as its subject — footage of successes is not a measurement of success rates. And ask whether both sides independently reached the same conclusion, which is why lesson 9 is the strongest thing on this map and this one is worth reading before the rest.
